body: The popular "use Claude/ChatGPT to analyze stocks" workflow is filing-first and adversarial: upload the primary documents (annual report, earnings deck, call transcripts), run a fixed library of saved prompts (business model, segments, moat, bull/bear/pre-mortem, forensic red flags, short-seller critique, management questions), and verify every number. Agentic variants (Claude Cowork/Code) add scheduled watchlist scans and Alpaca-connected paper-trading bots, but none of these come with a verified track record.
title: ai_tools_workflows › Takeaway

body: Professional fundamental shops run a repeatable pipeline: generate ideas (screens, special situations, filings, deal flow), state an explicit **variant perception** against consensus with a **catalyst**, test it hard (bull/bear debate, pre-mortem, management and channel work, and alternative data at larger funds), then size it. Their edge comes from a disciplined process and from how they size positions. It does not come from certainty. Several popular idea sources (spin-offs, 13F cloning) have weaker or decaying evidence than folklore suggests.
title: institutional_process › Takeaway

body:
- Retail-replicable quant: a rules-based multi-factor screen (quality + value + momentum, excluding junk/high leverage), rebalanced quarterly or semi-annually. In India, NSE factor indices and ETFs (e.g., Nifty200 Momentum 30, Alpha Low-Vol, Quality 30) offer cheap implementation.
- Not replicable: HFT and short-horizon stat-arb need co-location, direct exchange feeds, very low trading costs, leverage, and huge clean datasets. The RenTec example shows that even its own external funds can't reproduce Medallion.

body:
- O'Neil: sell any stock that falls 7-8% below purchase price, no exceptions. — [Liberated Stock Trader: CANSLIM](https://www.liberatedstocktrader.com/what-is-canslim/) [F]
- Qullamaggie: risk ≤0.5% per trade typically, 1% max; win rate ~25-30%. — [CTE research sheet](https://completetradersedge.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/CTE-Research-Sheet-Kristjan-Kullamagi-market-wizards-next-generation.pdf) [F]
- Minervini (*Trade Like a Stock Market Wizard*, *Think & Trade Like a Champion*): max stop 10%, average loss target ~5-6%; risk per trade ~1.25-2.5% of equity; 4-6 positions typical when fully invested (concentration), up to 10-12 max; "progressive exposure" — start small after losses and raise size only as trades work; never let a good-sized gain turn into a loss. [K] — summarized at [Chartmill SEPA](https://www.chartmill.com/documentation/trading-and-investing/methodologies/523-SEPA-Explained-Mark-Minervinis-Specific-Entry-Point-Analysis-System)
- Van Tharp (*Trade Your Way to Financial Freedom*): R = initial risk per share (entry − stop); every outcome measured as an R-multiple; expectancy = mean R-multiple across trades; "position sizing" is the key to meeting objectives; SQN (system quality number) = √N × mean(R)/stdev(R). [K] — [Van Tharp Institute](https://www.vantharp.com/) (not fetched)
- Expectancy formula: E = (Win% × Avg Win) − (Loss% × Avg Loss). Example: 30% win rate, avg win 5R, avg loss 1R → E = 0.30×5 − 0.70×1 = +0.8R per trade. [arithmetic]
- Kelly criterion: f* = W − (1 − W)/R, where W = win probability and R = avg win/avg loss (payoff ratio); full Kelly maximizes long-run log growth but has very large drawdowns and is highly sensitive to estimation error, so practitioners use fractional Kelly (¼-½). Half Kelly gives ~75% of the growth rate with roughly half the volatility. — [Wikipedia: Kelly criterion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kelly_criterion) [K]. Worked example: W = 0.30, R = 5 → f* = 0.30 − 0.70/5 = 0.16 (16% of capital *at risk* per bet — far above the 0.5-1% practitioners use, showing how fractional/conservative real sizing is).
- Pyramiding (Livermore/O'Neil/Darvas): add only after the initial position shows a profit, in decreasing size (e.g., O'Neil: initial buy, then add ~2-3% higher, total buys within ~5% of the pivot); never average down. — [Wikipedia: Jesse Livermore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jesse_Livermore) [K]
- Drawdown math (required gain to recover = 1/(1−d) − 1): −10% → +11.1%; −20% → +25%; −25% → +33.3%; −33% → +50%; −50% → +100%; −75% → +300%; −90% → +900%. [arithmetic]
- Losing streaks: with a 30% win rate, probability of 10 straight losers = 0.7^10 ≈ 2.8%; over 500 trades, such streaks are near-certain. At 1% risk, 10 losses ≈ −9.6% drawdown; at 5% risk, ≈ −40%. [arithmetic]

body:
`insight:sector-cycle-clock-nov-2026` · confidence: single-source

This is a snapshot of where each sector stands, built from Q2 FY27 results and Oct 2026 data. It is not a recommendation. Credit is in an upcycle (bank credit ~18–19% YoY, NBFC credit 15.4%), but private-bank NIMs are compressing (HDFC Bank 3.16%), PSBs lead on profit growth, and Nifty Bank traded at 1.63x P/B in Oct 2026, below its median. IT is at a growth trough (Infosys +1.5% CC YoY, guidance cut to 1–2%) with P/E ~18x against a 27x 7-year median (Jun 2026), and the debate is cyclical against structural (GenAI deflation). Pharma is the only large-cap sector above its FY26 average valuation, with the Section 232 generics review a tail risk. Specialty chemicals are past the trough in volumes but have no pricing power (CRISIL ~6% growth). Autos had a strong wholesale October (+12–16%), and the auto P/E of ~24x is near its long-term average. In capital goods, order inflows are at records (L&T ₹1.48 lakh cr) but transformer margins have peaked. In power, demand is at records (270.8 GW) and renewable additions have slowed to ~50 GW in FY27. Cement prices are recovering after a weak Q2 (UltraTech ₹974/t). Steel is in a margin upswing behind the safeguard duty. FMCG value growth is at a six-quarter high, led by rural, with the P/E below its median. QSR LFL is recovering slowly. Housing sales are flat to +3%. EMS margins are compressing after PLI. In defence, approvals are high but conversion is slow, at ~32–42x forward. Alcobev shows a premium–popular divide.

**snapshot:**
- banks: credit upcycle, NIM compression, P/B below median
- it: growth trough, P/E below median
- pharma: above-average valuation, tariff tail risk
- chemicals: volume recovery, price cap
- autos: strong wholesale, near-average P/E
- capgoods: record orders, product-margin peak
- power: record demand
- cement: price recovery H2
- steel: margin upswing (protection)
- fmcg: rural-led recovery
- qsr: slow LFL recovery
- realty: flat sales
- ems: post-PLI margin squeeze
- defence: approvals > orders, rich multiples
- alcobev: premium-popular divide
**as_of:** 2026-11-19

body:
`insight:buffett-moats-and-change` | confidence: verified | date: 1996-03-01

1995 letter: 'In business, I look for economic castles protected by unbreachable "moats."' (GEICO's moat widened as expenses fell to 23.6% of premiums). 1996: GEICO's 'economies of scale ... should allow us to maintain or even widen the protective moat'; its 'sustainable cost advantage' is what attracted him in 1951. 1987 letter on unglamorous holdings: 'Severe change and exceptional returns usually don't mix. Most investors, of course, behave as if just the opposite were true', conferring 'the highest price-earnings ratios on exotic-sounding businesses that hold out the promise of feverish change.' And: 'a business that constantly encounters major change also encounters many chances for major error ... economic terrain that is forever shifting violently is ground on which it is difficult to build a fortress-like business franchise. Such a franchise is usually the key to sustained high returns.' 1989 acquisition criteria: 'demonstrated consistent earning power (future projections are of little interest to us, nor are "turnaround" situations)', good ROE with little debt, 'simple businesses (if there's lots of technology, we won't understand it)'. Actionable: weight 'stable industry + widening cost or brand advantage' over 'disruption story'; check whether the moat is widening (falling unit cost vs peers, rising share) each year rather than assuming it.

Sources:
- https://www.berkshirehathaway.com/letters/1987.html
- https://www.berkshirehathaway.com/letters/1995.html
- https://www.berkshirehathaway.com/letters/1996.html
- https://www.berkshirehathaway.com/letters/1989.html

body:
`insight:good-numbers-too-good` · verified

RULE: treat these 'green flags' as hypotheses too. (1) SMOOTHNESS: earnings steadier than the businesses' cycles allow, with regular small beats (GE for years before 2017-18). (2) MARGIN/ROCE OUTLIERS: margins or ROCE far above every peer in a commodity-like or low-ticket business (Vakrangee ~25% OPM and ~40% ROCE in rural kiosks; Wirecard margins from partners it did not control). (3) GROWTH ABOVE THE LEADER: a small player outgrowing the category leader with no new channel, technology or price advantage (Manpasand vs Parle Agro's Frooti; Ricoh India growing far faster than its own parent). (4) IMPROVING UNIT ECONOMICS THAT CAN'T BE CHECKED outside company reports (Luckin's items per order, refuted by store video). (5) CHEAP + OPAQUE: low P/E with thin disclosure and auditor churn (Rajesh Exports). (6) CLEAN CASH THAT DOESN'T EARN (Satyam). (7) EPS GROWTH VIA DEALS + non-GAAP adjustments (Valeant). (8) LOW NPAs IN A FAST-GROWING LOAN BOOK (Yes Bank, DHFL). COMMON THREAD: each good number could only be verified through the company's own accounts; outsiders had no independent read (store counts, subscriber data, sovereign payments, industry volumes). TEST: for every standout metric ask 'what mechanism produces this, and what outside data would show it?'. If none exists, the number gets no credit until it does.

**Not supported in 2021–2024 for this simple public rule.** Against size-matched random controls drawn
on the same dates, 849 cluster events (ex-biotech) earned **0.0% mean / −3.9% median excess over 12 months**
(95% month-clustered bootstrap CI for the mean **−4.8% to +5.0%**; hit rate 44.9%). At 6 months: −0.3% mean
(CI −3.3% to +2.6%). The CI is wide enough to hide a small effect (~+2–4%/yr) but rules out an effect of
the size Cohen–Malloy–Pomorski report for *opportunistic* insiders (~10%/yr) for this unfiltered rule, even
after a generous survivorship correction (see §6). **As a standalone screen it is not an edge for us.** At most it is
a weak tilt / research-queue prioritiser; any real edge would have to come from extra filtering
(opportunistic vs routine, buy size vs holdings, governance, banks) that this test did not establish.

- **Method:** sector cycle/lead indicator · **P(ours)** 0.55 · **P(base)** 0.45 · resolve by 2027-02-28
- **Evidence:** Q2 FY27 call (30-Oct-2026): record revenue ₹3,091 cr (+61%), EBITDA ₹643 cr (+187%), margin ~21%; Phenolics revenue ₹2,291 cr, EBIT ₹515 cr, 'principal driver… disruptions to international supply chains, higher landed cost of imports' (West Asia); H1 Phenolics EBIT ₹933 cr already above best-ever full year (FY22 ₹867 cr). Advanced Intermediates EBIT fell to ₹49 cr (6%); CFO guided Q3 AI EBIT% 'between Q1 and Q2, closer to Q1', Q4 better. New DCTL chlorination/photohalogenation assets commissioned end-Q2. Screener OP: Q3 FY26 211, Q4 FY26 376, Q1 FY27 540, Q2 FY27 627 (₹ cr).
- **Why our number differs from base:** Lead indicator: phenol/acetone spreads are being held up by import disruption that was still in place into Q3 (Brent Q4-to-date ~$103 vs Q3 ~$91.5), while AI segment guidance points up and new assets add volume. A 20% fall from Q2 is needed to miss. We lean above the mean-reversion base.
- **Base-rate reasoning:** After a record spread-driven quarter, Indian commodity-chemical makers see a ≥20% sequential operating-profit fall roughly half the time or more; naive P(OP ≥ ₹500 cr) ~45%.
- **Resolution rule:** YES if Deepak Nitrite's consolidated Operating Profit (screener.in quarterly table; equivalently EBITDA excluding other income) for the quarter ended 31-Dec-2026 is ≥₹500 cr.

- **id:** `thesis:paper-call:US-JPM:initial-fy27-nii-guide-110bn-plus`
- **Method:** management-tone-vs-delivery · **P(ours)** 0.38 · **P(base)** 0.45 · resolve by 2027-01-31
- **Evidence:** Q3 2026 earnings release (Oct-2026): net revenue $50.9bn (+8%), NII $27.1bn (+13%), NII ex-Markets $24.7bn (+6%); net income $15.3bn; Dimon: 'large fiscal deficits, sticky inflation, elevated asset prices, rising interest rates and geopolitical conditions continue to shift under the surface… we remain prepared for a wide range of outcomes.' SEC XBRL (InterestIncomeExpenseNet, GAAP): Q1 2026 $25.37bn, Q2 $25.51bn, Q3 $27.04bn (9M $77.9bn) vs FY2025 $95.44bn. US 10-yr ~4.9–5.1% (Yahoo ^TNX).
- **Why our number differs from base:** Management-tone test: JPM's outlook language is habitually cautious and its January NII guides have tended to sit close to the Q4 run-rate ×4 (history from memory, unverified). Q3 ×4 is ~$108bn; reaching a ≥$110bn guide needs a Q4 step-up plus explicit growth assumptions that Dimon's tone argues against. We lean below base.
- **Base-rate reasoning:** Naive: initial guide ≈ Q4 2026 NII ×4; with Q4 likely ~$27–27.5bn, ≥$110bn needs a guide above run-rate — roughly 45%.
- **Resolution rule:** YES if the firmwide (total, managed basis) FY2027 NII outlook in JPM's Q4 2026 earnings presentation/call is ≥$110bn ('~$110bn' or a range with midpoint ≥$110bn counts). If only NII ex-Markets is guided, add the stated Markets NII assumption if given; otherwise void.
- **Resolution source:** JPMorgan Chase Q4 2026 earnings presentation / call (jpmorganchase.com IR) and 8-K
- **Sources used:** https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/19617/000162828026065582/a3q26erfexhibit991narrative.htm; https://data.sec.gov/api/xbrl/companyconcept/CIK0000019617/us-gaap/InterestIncomeExpenseNet.json
